summary: SDK head-of-line blocking in pipelined client causes serialized requests, high tail latency and timeouts for enterprise tenant
description: Issue summary: Customer reports a sudden increase in tail latency and 504s during routine batch inference. Symptoms point to client-side request serialization rather than serving-runtime slowdown. Impact: customer production pipelines observe ~95th-99th percentile latency spikes and intermittent timeouts for multi-request pipelines.
steps_to_reproduce: 2) Configure SDK with connectionPool.max=2 and default retry/backoff jitter enabled (default customer config).
3) Start 50 concurrent client worker threads issuing streaming chat completions to the same tenant and model; each request keeps an open streaming connection for ~4s.

4) Observe that requests appear to serialize at the SDK level: only a few requests are active to the gateway while others are queued in user-space, producing long queue waits and some 504s after client-side timeout.
logs: [2026-03-10T08:14:21Z] INFO client-sdk ConnectionPool.acquire waited=421ms in queue (max=2, in_use=2)
[2026-03-10T08:14:21Z] WARN client-sdk RetryManager retrying request id=abcd-1234 attempt=3 backoff=1500ms jitter=+500ms
[2026-03-10T08:14:22Z] ERROR api-gateway 504 upstream_timeout tenant=acme-dataworks request_id=abcd-1234 elapsed_ms=5100
investigation_notes: Initial hypothesis: serving-runtime tail regression. Investigated and ruled out by comparing per-node p99 CPU/GPU and token throughput — no corresponding spike on the cluster for this tenant.

Reproduction in staging with load generator showed identical symptom when SDK connectionPool.max <= 2 and retry/backoff configuration active: queued requests accumulate in SDK before hitting API gateway (head-of-line blocking).

Root cause: SDK's pipeline implementation serializes streaming handshakes while a single socket holder is performing a retry/backoff; internal semaphore is held for longer than necessary while jitter/backoff timers run, preventing other concurrent requests from acquiring sockets. This effectively reduces concurrency below the configured max and causes user-space queuing and client timeouts.

Observed metrics supporting this: client_connection_wait_seconds.percentile(99)=0.48s, sdk_outbound_queue_length > 40, api_gateway_active_connections remained steady at expected levels (no gateway saturation).
workaround: Short term (immediate) - Instruct customer to increase SDK connectionPool.max to >= 10 and reduce per-request client timeout to allow longer upstream windows.
If changing pool size is not possible: disable client jitter or set retry.max_attempts=1 to avoid long in-process backoffs that hold semaphores.
Redirect some traffic to a separate tenant/model shard to spread concurrent streaming connections across more gateway workers.
Support has applied a temporary rate-limiter rule on the tenant to keep active concurrent streams per second within safe bounds while patch is prepared.
resolution: Engineering has created a patch to release for redwood-sdk-java v1.4.2 which changes the pipeline locking so backoff timers do not hold the socket acquisition semaphore and adds a non-blocking connection attempt path.
Planned release: v1.4.2 staged rollout beginning 2026-03-13 with Canary to 5% of enterprise customers, full rollout 2026-03-15 pending telemetry.
Post-release, customer should revert temporary SDK config changes (connectionPool.max can be lowered back to original documented defaults) and remove tenant rate-limiter rule.

follow_up_tasks: 1) Engineering: Release SDK v1.4.2 and monitor connection_wait_percentile and sdk_outbound_queue metrics for 48h post-rollout.
2) Developer Experience: Update SDK docs to recommend default connectionPool.max=10 for streaming-heavy workloads and document retry/backoff interactions.
3) Observability: Add alert when client_connection_wait_seconds.p99 > 300ms and when sdk_outbound_queue_length > 20 for any tenant.
4) Support: Contact affected customers with mitigation steps and coordinate upgrade windows.
5) Product: Consider adding server-side soft-queueing to smooth short surges to avoid client-side semaphore contention in future releases.
